title: Fetal monitoring (CTG)
what: A recording of your baby's heartbeat and the tightening of your womb. Two sensors on belts are placed on your belly. It is safe for you and your baby.
why: Usually from week 32 of pregnancy, to check on your baby. Also during labor, if the baby moves less, and for other reasons your doctor gives.
duration: usually 20 to 40 minutes, sometimes up to an hour
tell_doctor: If your baby is moving less
If you have contractions, pain, discharge, or leaking fluid

prepare.title: Food
prepare.text: Eat 1 to 2 hours before the test. Do not come hungry. Babies are usually more active after you eat.

prepare.title: Before the test
prepare.text: Use the toilet. You will lie down for a while.

prepare.title: Clothes
prepare.text: Wear something comfortable that lets you uncover your belly easily.

steps: You lie on your side or half sitting up. Lying flat on your back for long is best avoided
Gel goes on your belly, and two sensors are held in place with belts
One sensor listens to the baby's heart, the other measures your womb tightening
Sometimes you get a button. Press it when the baby moves
The machine records on paper or a screen
If the baby is asleep, the recording may take longer
feel: Nothing unpleasant, just the belts pressing and the cool gel
You will hear your baby's heartbeat
after: A doctor reads the recording, usually right away or the same day
If the result is unclear, the test may be repeated. Most often the baby was just asleep
You can go back to your day straight away
red_flags: Your baby is moving much less or has stopped moving
Regular contractions or strong belly pain
A bad headache, spots before your eyes, or swelling: call emergency services or your maternity hospital

faq.q: Is CTG harmful to my baby?
faq.a: No. The sensor uses weak ultrasound, like a regular ultrasound scan. It is safe to do many times.

faq.q: Why was I told to repeat the CTG?
faq.a: Most often the baby was asleep, so the recording was quiet. It is usually repeated after you eat or take a walk.
